blocks.html: There is no difference in the ancient Hebrew spelling of these three words yerach, yaw-ray’akh or Yārēach.
blocks.text: There is no difference in the ancient Hebrew spelling of these three words yerach, yaw-ray’akh or Yārēach.

blocks.html: The reason that the Strongs Concordance gives them three separate numbers is because, even though they were spelled the exact same, there was a difference in pronunciation depending on if you were using the word “moon” in poetry or just as a relative statement.
blocks.text: The reason that the Strongs Concordance gives them three separate numbers is because, even though they were spelled the exact same, there was a difference in pronunciation depending on if you were using the word “moon” in poetry or just as a relative statement.

blocks.html: Psalms is a book of poetry, so when the word “moon” is used in the text it is believed to be pronounced “yaw-ray’akh”. The book of Melakim/Kings is not poetry, and thus the word “yerach” is used.
blocks.text: Psalms is a book of poetry, so when the word “moon” is used in the text it is believed to be pronounced “yaw-ray’akh”. The book of Melakim/Kings is not poetry, and thus the word “yerach” is used.

blocks.html: After the invention of Hebrew vowel points, the Hebrew language was able to show the difference in pronunciation, which gives rise to the reason why we seemingly have two words for “moon” in Hebrew represented in the Strongs Concordance.
